scribe_response.text: Tell me about someone who mattered a great deal in your life. The most important person in my life is my husband Ramon. I was twenty-two and teaching my first, first class in a village school outside Iloilo. He was twenty-five, a ship's cook, home on leave after a long voyage. We met at church on a rainy Sunday, with everyone crowded, everyone crowded under the porch roof. I was holding my father's huge black umbrella, um which was broken on one side. Ramon stood next to me, soaked to the skin, and said my umbrella looked brave. I told him it was only, was only stubborn, and he laughed so loudly the priest turned around. He walked me home that afternoon, carrying the umbrella and describing the places he had seen. He had been to Hamburg, Rotterdam, and Singapore, and he remembered the food in um each. I had never left the island, so I listened as if to fairy tales. What I noticed first were his, were his hands, big and burned by the kitchen. Those were the hands of a man who feeds people, and I trusted them at once. He courted me for two years, writing from ports all over the world on thin blue paper. What happened next? Each letter smelled faintly of cinnamon and diesel, and I kept them in a shoebox. When he came um home he cooked for my whole family, and my mother approved after one plate. My father was harder to please, but Ramon um fixed a leaking boat for him, and that settled it. We married in the same church where we met, on a bright morning in March. My hands shook so badly that I dropped the ring. Ramon picked it up and said it was a sign we would never lose each other. Life with a seafarer is not easy, because he is always leaving or arriving. For nearly thirty years our marriage was a series of airport goodbyes and joyful homecomings. I raised the children mostly alone, and I learned to fix a um roof and argue with a landlord. Ramon sent money and long letters, and later recorded tapes of his voice telling bedtime stories. Liza and Paolo listened to those tapes until the ribbon wore thin. When he was home he took over the kitchen, and the flat smelled of garlic and ginger. He is a gentle man who never um raises his voice, not even about a crashed motorbike. He just sat down on the step and asked the boy how he planned to pay. Can you tell me more about that? When the ships grew old and he grew tired, he retired and came home for good. It was strange at first, because we had spent so many years waiting for each other. We had to learn how to eat breakfast together um and how to be silent in one room. Now he keeps herbs on our balcony and talks to the basil as if it were a child. Every evening we sit there, drink tea, and watch the lights come on across the city. I have asked myself why our marriage lasted, and I think it was the letters. Writing gave us time to think about what we uh wanted to say. Ramon taught me that love is a daily practice, like cooking, and needs fresh ingredients. He also taught me um that a person can be far away and still beside you. When I look at his hands now, they are um spotted and a little shaky. They are still the same hands that held my broken umbrella. I would choose that rainy Sunday again without a moment of hesitation. Even now, when thunder rolls um over the city, he reaches for my hand. I think a good marriage is mostly patience and a hot meal.
